posts.title: A Sunday ambient hour
posts.excerpt: Once a month Nanami keeps the booth door open on Sunday afternoon and plays one side after another, quietly, for whoever comes up the steps.
posts.content:
Once a month Nanami keeps the booth door open on Sunday afternoon and plays one side after another, quietly, for whoever comes up the steps.

What played

Warm Static, both sides; then the first side of Paper Lanterns, Slow Rain, with the rain outside doing half the work.

Nobody talks much. People sit on the step by the door or browse the folk rack with the sound behind them.

Next time

The first Sunday of November, from three. Free, no booking; the booth itself stays bookable before and after.

The point is not to sell anything. It is to remember what a whole side sounds like.

Nanami Kurose

posts.title: How we grade a record
posts.excerpt: Every used record in the shop is graded twice: once under the lamp, once on the booth turntable. A note on what Mint, Near Mint, VG+ and VG mean here.
posts.content:
Every used record in the shop is graded twice: once under the lamp, once on the booth turntable. A note on what Mint, Near Mint, VG+ and VG mean here.

Under the lamp

Tetsuo tilts the disc under a small lamp and looks for hairlines, scuffs and anything deeper. A mark you can feel with a fingernail is never better than VG.

On the turntable

Then the record is cleaned and played through, both sides, with headphones. A clean-looking disc can still crackle; a scuffed one can play silently. The ear decides.

On the card

The grade goes on the catalogue card with the number, the year and where the record came from. If we are unsure between two grades, we choose the lower one.

posts.title: A box of 1970s folk from an estate
posts.excerpt: Forty records from one house in the hills: folk albums from the early 1970s, kept upright, in order, for fifty years.
posts.content:
Forty records from one house in the hills: folk albums from the early 1970s, kept upright, in order, for fifty years.

The box

The family rang in August. The records were in a cedar box under the stairs, each one in a paper inner sleeve with the date of purchase written on it in pencil.

Most are VG+, a few Near Mint. Songs from the Upper Field is the one we kept playing at the counter.

In the shop

They are on the new-arrivals shelf this month, filed under HBK-0340 to HBK-0379. One copy of each.

posts.title: A new stylus for the booth
posts.excerpt: The booth turntable got a new stylus this week. Why we change it every year, and what a worn needle does to a record.
posts.content:
The booth turntable got a new stylus this week. Why we change it every year, and what a worn needle does to a record.

Why it matters

A worn stylus sounds dull at first, then starts to chip at the groove walls. In a booth that plays six hours a day, a year is enough.

What you will hear

Brighter cymbals, quieter run-outs and less hiss at the end of a side. If you graded a record in the booth last month, it may sound a little better now.

posts.title: Jazz on a wet Thursday
posts.excerpt: Rain kept the street empty, so the booth ran one record after another: six quiet jazz sides for a wet afternoon.
posts.content:
Rain kept the street empty, so the booth ran one record after another: six quiet jazz sides for a wet afternoon.

The stack

Low Tide Hours, side B; Blue Hour at Minase, side A; then four from the used racks, chosen by whoever was in the booth.

The rule on a wet Thursday: no record faster than a walk.

posts.title: Twenty years in the lane
posts.excerpt: The shop opened in 2006 in the lane behind the bakery, with Tetsuo's own records and a borrowed turntable. A short note on twenty years.
posts.content:
The shop opened in 2006 in the lane behind the bakery, with Tetsuo's own records and a borrowed turntable. A short note on twenty years.

The first rack

One rack of jazz, one of folk and a box of singles by the door. The turntable was lent by a friend who never asked for it back.

Now

Six racks, one booth, about four thousand records and one clerk who knows them better than the owner does.

Records come back. People who bought something here in 2006 sell it back to us now, and someone else takes it home.

Tetsuo Hayami
